einzeiler: Why small-cap stocks are outperforming large caps amid AI and biotech speculation
kurzfassung: Small-cap stocks have recently outperformed large caps for the first time in years, largely driven by speculative excitement around AI and biotechnology. Guest Dan Rasmussen explains how market liquidity, financing conditions, and private equity valuations impact these smaller companies. The episode also previews upcoming crucial economic data, including the jobs report and inflation numbers.
stichpunkte: Markets await upcoming U.S. jobs and CPI reports to gauge Federal Reserve interest rate decisions
Nvidia reported a strong quarter with projected 70% revenue growth, though long-term sustainability and circular financing spark debate
Small-cap stocks have beaten large caps over the past 12 months, driven by speculative excitement in semiconductors and biotech
Dan Rasmussen explains that venture-capital-style unprofitable small caps have led the rally due to low market liquidity
High-yield credit spreads are near all-time lows, making financing extremely cheap for risky borrowers
Private equity firms face a major exit logjam because they acquired companies at high EBITDA multiples compared to current public market valuations
The S&P 600 includes profitability filters unlike the Russell 2000, making it a stronger choice for long-term buy-and-hold investors
Vanguard Total Market Index offers broader exposure than the S&P 500, avoiding arbitrary size cutoffs

clips.text: Nvidia reported stellar financial results and projected massive revenue growth for the upcoming fiscal year, noting that supply chain constraints are the primary bottleneck.
The hosts examine the remarkable 12-month performance figures for the small-cap index, contrasting profitable and loss-making segments within the market.

clips.hook: High-yield credit spreads near all-time lows
clips.text: High-yield credit spreads have dropped below 300 basis points, reflecting historically cheap borrowing conditions for risky and smaller enterprises.

clips.hook: Private equity firms paying 17 times EBITDA
clips.text: Dan Rasmussen points out that private equity portfolios are heavily weighed down because assets were acquired at excessively high EBITDA multiples.

clips.hook: The efficient markets hypothesis and geographic weighting
clips.text: Passive investing strategies should align with the efficient markets hypothesis by adopting a market-cap-weighted approach across global regions.

beschreibung:
On this week’s episode of WSJ’s Take On the Week, host Miriam Gottfried and guest host Aaron Back, editor of WSJ’s Heard on the Street, preview the upcoming employment and inflation releases in advance of the Federal Open Market Committee’s September policy meeting. They analyze why these economic indicators will draw heightened focus under Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. Then Miriam and Aaron dig into Nvidia’s recent blowout earnings and whether we will see that echo in Broadcom’s earnings this week.

Next, Dan Rasmussen, founder and portfolio manager at Verdad Advisers, offers insight into the past year's small-cap stock surge following an extended period of underperformance relative to mega-caps. Rasmussen explains why private equity firms face a massive exit logjam from acquisitions of small companies due to inflated valuations. Finally, we ask Rasmussen: does value investing still work?

This is WSJ’s Take On the Week where co-hosts Telis Demos, writer for WSJ’s Heard on the Street, and Miriam Gottfried, WSJ’s investing and wealth management reporter, cut through the noise and dive into markets, the economy and finance—the big trades, key players and business news ahead.
